problem: Zero-shot foundation-model ObjectNav agents are developed and evaluated in synchronous simulators where the world pauses during inference, so latency is free and sequential perception-reasoning-action pipelines are never penalized. Under wall-clock budgets their performance is overestimated and degrades.
motivation: On real robots inference latency causes pause-and-go behavior and consumes task time, yet standard metrics (SR under a step budget, SPL) ignore it. The authors observe that heavier VLM/LLM methods degrade sharply once inference time counts, and argue this is an architectural problem: a single sequential loop lets the slowest module set the reactivity of the whole system.
key_idea: Evaluate ObjectNav with a ROS2 real-time asynchronous stepping layer over Habitat, and build RTNav, a modular agent whose perception, mapping, planning and navigation threads run at their own rates while a VLM is called only on demand.
insight: Most of the degradation comes from latency in heavy modules: light methods (VLFM, L3MVN) lose 1-2 SR points, while BeliefMapNav drops 38.2 on HM3D-v1 and 36.8 on HM3D-v2 in SR. Decoupling detection from reasoning gives >20x more unique detection frames per second and 14%+ less idle time. The VLM ablation shows the VLM must still be capable enough: Qwen3.5-4B gets 37.8 SR vs 72.3 for 9B, whereas hardware changes barely alter SR/SPL (Jetson Thor SR 72.2).
method: Real-time ObjectNav benchmark: a ROS2 environment node hosts Habitat at fixed 30 Hz wall-clock stepping and the agent node publishes velocity commands (v, ω) asynchronously. The stale command stays active during inference. A sync mode reproduces standard Habitat for a controlled comparison.

Discrete-to-continuous action mapping: baselines' discrete actions become velocities (0.25 m/s forward, 30°/s turn), so 500 sync steps roughly equal a 500 s real-time budget. The budget is 500 s in real mode.

Perception: OWLv2 detects at ~15 Hz with a vocabulary of the target, VLM-generated synonyms and 399 LVIS categories. Qwen3.5-9B verifies candidates (yes/no first-token probability >0.90) and MobileSAM refines masks. A persistent object graph confirms objects after 3 distinct viewpoints.
Mapping: back-projects RGB-D into a point cloud and a 2D metric map with obstacles, explored area, frontiers (VLFM extraction) and confirmed targets.

Planning: when no target is confirmed, the VLM sees each frontier's latest RGB view with red line/arrow overlays and picks the most promising one. It is queried only when replanning is needed (frontier reached, invalid or vanished). The agent starts each episode with a 360° rotation.

Navigation: a PointNav policy drives to the current frontier or confirmed target while other modules run, communicating through a shared state bus. In the real world it is replaced by an FMM planner + PD controller.
Efficiency engineering: cached text embeddings, batched multi-view inference, GPU memory coordination, C++ extensions for post-processing and 2D-to-3D projection.

results: Under real-time evaluation RTNav gets the highest SR on all three benchmarks (61.8 on HM3D-v1, 72.3 on HM3D-v2, 44.6 on OVON) and the best SCT. It beats the strongest baselines, evaluated synchronously, by 10.5, 9.1 and 6.4 SR points respectively. Its SPL is comparable to VLFM (OVON SPL is lower: 21.1 vs 23.7). Baselines such as BeliefMapNav collapse under real-time (SR 65.5→27.3 on HM3D-v1).
limitations: Focuses on static environments and object navigation; extension to locomotion, manipulation and dynamic scenes is left for future work

Real-time results depend on hardware speed (SCT drops on Jetson Thor), and baselines are re-implemented with dependency and version changes (reproduced numbers differ from reported ones, e.g. L3MVN on HM3D-v2)
Real-world evaluation is qualitative (16 target objects, no quantitative results in the text)
